blocks.text: Bacteria use different motility patterns to navigate and explore their natural habitats: flagellar movement, twitching (crawling), gliding, sliding, Brownian movement and movement by an axial filament.

Most bacilli and spirilla move by means of flagella: they swim. When a whole bacterial population moves together by means of flagella, the movement is called swarming. Flagellar movement lets bacteria travel in liquid media. Counter-clockwise rotation of the flagellum pushes the cell forward with the flagellum trailing behind.
Twitching is used to move over surfaces. It is mediated by pili, which bind to the surrounding solid surface and then retract, so the bacterial cell is pulled forward.
Gliding is similar to twitching. In gliding, bacteria secrete a slimy substance that helps them glide smoothly over solid surfaces.
Sliding is due to the expansion created by the pushing force of dividing cells.

blocks.alt: Five panels. Swimming: one rod-shaped cell in liquid with a bundle of flagella trailing behind. Swarming: a group of cells moving together, each with trailing flagella. Twitching: a cell on a surface with its pilus stretched ahead; label Pilus retracts. Gliding: a cell on a surface leaving a grey trail; label Slimy substance. Sliding: a row of dividing cells on a surface with a new cell added and arrows pointing outwards both ways.

blocks.text: Some bacteria that have neither flagella nor pili, such as Streptococcus, move because of the random and uncontrolled movements of the particles in the fluid around them.

Some bacteria, the spirochaetes, have a modified flagellum known as an axial filament. It is anchored at one end and runs lengthwise in the periplasmic space (between the cell membrane and the outer membrane). It consists of two sets of flagella-like fibrils anchored at the two poles of the cell. The axial filament helps spirochaetes with flexing, swimming, creeping and spinning movements.

blocks.alt: A long spiral spirochaete cell drawn as a curving S. A yellow axial filament winds along the whole length of the cell just beneath its outer layer. Labels: Cell wall, Axial filament.
